claim: Kahneman and Klein: judging an intuition's likely quality needs an assessment of how predictable the environment is and whether the person could learn its regularities.
quote: evaluating the likely quality of an intuitive judgment requires an assessment of the predictability of the environment
authors: Kahneman D, Klein G
title: Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
transfer: Router step: trust the first answer only when the task class is regular and a real check exists; doubt on open or low-validity tasks.

claim: Subjective confidence is not a reliable indicator of accuracy, per the Kahneman and Klein review.
quote: Subjective experience is not a reliable indicator of judgment accuracy.
authors: Kahneman D, Klein G
title: Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
transfer: Do not gate on stated confidence; gate on agreement across attempts and check results.

claim: Mechanical (formula) prediction beat clinical judgment on average by about 10% accuracy; clinicians were substantially better in only 6-16% of studies.
quote: On average, mechanical-prediction techniques were about 10% more accurate than clinical predictions.
authors: Grove WM, Zald DH, Lebow BS, Snitz BE, Nelson C
title: Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis
n: number of studies not stated in abstract
transfer: Where a checker or scoring rule exists, let the program combine evidence (votes, tests) instead of the model's holistic judgment of its own candidates.

claim: Mechanical prediction substantially outperformed clinical prediction in 33-47% of studies examined.
quote: mechanical prediction substantially outperformed clinical prediction in 33%-47% of studies examined
authors: Grove WM, Zald DH, Lebow BS, Snitz BE, Nelson C
title: Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis
transfer: Prefer fixed selectors (symmetry check, test pass rate) over free-form self-judgment at selection time.

claim: Einstellung: the first idea triggered by familiar features blocks a better solution, and expert chess players who said they were searching for better kept looking at features of the first solution (eye tracking).
quote: their eye movements showed that they continued to look at features of the problem related to the solution
authors: Bilalic M, McLeod P, Gobet F
title: Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect
transfer: Asking a model to look for a better answer may not change what it attends to; force a restated problem view or a rival built from ignored features, on open tasks only.

claim: Einstellung boundary: when the familiar move was advantageous but suboptimal players kept looking at it; when it was a blunder most players disengaged. Experts who found the best move gradually disengaged.
quote: Experts who found the optimal move gradually disengage their attention from the Einstellung move.
authors: Sheridan H, Reingold EM
title: The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements
transfer: Forced-doubt steps pay only when the first answer is good but not best; they add harm when first answers are simply right (our ARC and word-puzzle data).

claim: Chess experts keep a memory advantage even for random material: the meta-analytic correlation between expertise and random-material recall was moderate and significant, seen in nearly every study (corrects the earlier brief's claim that the edge vanishes).
quote: the effect was observed in nearly every study
authors: Sala G, Gobet F
title: Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: A meta-analysis
n: not stated in abstract; numeric r lost in abstract text
transfer: Expertise is many small chunks; a lesson ledger should be many small tagged entries, not a few big rules.

claim: Chess templates: skilled memory also uses long-term retrieval structures beyond chunks, revising Chase-Simon theory.
quote: use long-term memory retrieval structures
authors: Gobet F, Simon HA
title: Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
transfer: Store lessons as pattern plus slots (signature, trick, trap) so one entry covers several similar problems.

claim: Deliberate practice explained 26% of performance variance in games (chess included), 21% music, 18% sports, 4% education, under 1% professions; it matters but less than argued.
quote: deliberate practice is important, but not as important as has been argued
authors: Macnamara BN, Hambrick DZ, Oswald FL
title: Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
n: number of studies not stated in abstract
transfer: Caution: expertise in less regular domains (professions) is weakly tied to practice; do not assume accumulated experience alone makes the ledger trustworthy.

claim: Feeling of rightness: initial intuitive answers carry a metacognitive signal; low feeling of rightness led to longer rethinking and more answer changes across four experiments.
quote: low FOR was associated with longer rethinking times and an increased probability of answer change
authors: Thompson VA, Prowse Turner JA, Pennycook G
title: Intuition, reason, and metacognition
transfer: Machine analogue: spend extra calls only when first-pass attempts disagree or the answer was not fluent; stop at the first answer when attempts agree.

claim: FOR judgments were predicted by how fluently the initial answer came to mind.
quote: FOR judgments were consistently predicted by how fluently the initial answer came to mind
authors: Thompson VA, Prowse Turner JA, Pennycook G
title: Intuition, reason, and metacognition
transfer: Fluency is a poor truth signal for a model too (samples are correlated); prefer measured agreement across independent probes plus checks.

claim: Mercier and Sperber argue the function of reasoning is argumentative: to devise and evaluate arguments meant to persuade, which explains confirmation bias and poor solo reasoning.
quote: Our hypothesis is that the function of reasoning is argumentative.
authors: Mercier H, Sperber D
title: Why do humans reason? Arguments for an argumentative theory
transfer: Separate proposer and critic calls; critic evaluates a candidate as someone else's, tied to a run or a differing input.

claim: LLMs cannot reliably self-correct reasoning without external feedback; performance sometimes worsens after self-correction.
quote: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
authors: Huang J, Chen X, Mishra S, Zheng HS, Yu AW, Song X, Zhou D
title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
transfer: Any review or pre-mortem step must be tied to an external signal (run, test, differing input) or it only adds doubt.

claim: Multiagent debate: several LLM instances propose and debate answers over rounds, improving math and strategy reasoning and reducing fallacious answers.
quote: significantly enhances mathematical and strategic reasoning across a number of tasks
authors: Du Y, Li S, Torralba A, Tenenbaum JB, Mordatch I
title: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
transfer: Debate is an option for open tasks; compare against equal-token self-consistency before adopting.

claim: LLM evaluators favor their own outputs, and self-preference correlates linearly with self-recognition ability after fine-tuning.
quote: a linear correlation between self-recognition capability and the strength of self-preference bias
authors: Panickssery A, Bowman SR, Feng S
title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
transfer: Strip authorship and shuffle order when a call judges candidates; the machine form of the argumentative-theory asymmetry.

claim: GPT-3 era models showed human-like intuitive errors; ChatGPT models mostly answered correctly and stayed accurate even when chain of thought was blocked.
quote: they remain accurate even when prevented from engaging in chain-of-thought reasoning
authors: Hagendorff T, Fabi S, Kosinski M
title: Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in large language models but disappeared in ChatGPT
n: GPT model family, cognitive reflection and semantic illusion tasks
transfer: For strong models, fast-vs-slow is not a clean switch; first answers on trap-style puzzles are often already right, supporting a trust-first default.

claim: An ensemble of 12 LLMs matched a crowd of 925 human forecasters on 31 binary questions; showing models the median human forecast raised accuracy 17-28%; blending human and machine forecasts was most accurate.
quote: the LLM crowd outperforms a no-information benchmark and is statistically indistinguishable from the human crowd
authors: Schoenegger P, Tuminauskaite I, Park PS, Bastos RVS, Tetlock PE
title: Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction capabilities rival human crowd accuracy
transfer: On forecasting-type open questions, aggregate several different models or prompts; mixed-model ensembles are less correlated than samples from one model.

claim: The implementation pre-mortem (prospective hindsight) papers the search surfaced are conceptual or qualitative; no controlled test that a pre-mortem improves decision quality was found (evidence gap).
quote: an implementation premortem is a tool that when combined with a structured analytic approach
authors: Wippold GM, Garcia KA, Domlyn A, Wong D, Fernandez ME
title: Proactive planning for contextual fit: the role of the implementation premortem
transfer: Treat pre-mortem as an untested step; run it only before costly actions and measure avoided bad runs per token.

claim: A 2026 survey of 225 Norwegian military personnel found endorsement of Klein's decision-making framework is not unidimensional (two attitude dimensions).
quote: These findings suggest that military professionals' endorsement of Klein's framework is not unidimensional
authors: Mattingsdal J
title: Assessing Military Professionals' Endorsement of Decision-Making Assumptions: An Exploratory Factor Analysis
transfer: none; shows recognition-primed claims are a bundle, not one tested effect.

claim: Tetlock's work found hedgehog-style experts predict worse than foxes (as described by a later commentary); the original book was not opened.
quote: Tetlock's finding that hedgehog experts are worse predictors than foxes
authors: Keil FC (describing Tetlock)
title: When and why do hedgehogs and foxes differ?
transfer: Many-angle aggregation (fox style) over one committed theory supports divergence on open forecasting tasks. No Tetlock 2005 numbers are claimed here.
